# nsite-clay

> A self-editable nsite. One HTML file holds a page's markup, styling, content
> and state, and republishes itself: the browser serialises the document, stores
> it on Blossom, and publishes a Nostr event saying which bytes are now the page.
> Relays hold the pointer, Blossom holds the bytes, and there is no server in
> between.

This file is the brief for an agent. If you are building someone a website with
nsite-clay, read all of it before you start. It is long on purpose: it tells you
what the thing is, what to ask for, which template to begin from, and what will
go wrong. It links the documentation rather than restating it.

- The guide, with screenshots, for the person you are building it for:
  https://nsite-clay.cypherpunk.today/guide.html
- The publisher, if they would rather do it themselves in a browser:
  https://nsite-clay.cypherpunk.today/deploy.html
- Templates, browsable: https://nsite-clay.cypherpunk.today/templates.html
- The block composer template, the one to read before writing a block library:
  https://nsite-clay.cypherpunk.today/t/cms/
- What a template must do: https://github.com/jooray/nsite-clay/blob/main/templates/_shared/CONTRACT.md
- Runtime reference: https://github.com/jooray/nsite-clay/blob/main/docs/RUNTIME-API.md
- Where state lives: https://github.com/jooray/nsite-clay/blob/main/docs/state.md
- Source: https://github.com/jooray/nsite-clay
- What an nsite is, from the people who built the idea: https://nsite.run

---

## 1. What an nsite is

An nsite is web hosting on Nostr. Not long-form notes rendered as a blog: whole
HTML files, with their CSS, their images and their JavaScript.

Three pieces, and none of them is a server you rent:

**Blossom** stores bytes and names them by their own SHA-256. Upload a file, get
back its hash. Ask any Blossom server for that hash and you get exactly those
bytes or nothing, because the name *is* the checksum. Content-addressed storage,
so a file cannot be quietly swapped for a different one.

**A Nostr event** maps paths to hashes. `/index.html` is this hash, `/about.html`
is that one. The event is signed by the site owner's key, and it is *replaceable*,
meaning a newer one from the same key supersedes it. Publishing a new one is the
deploy. This is [NIP-5A](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/5A.md),
kind 15128 for a key's main site and 35128 for a named one.

**A gateway** is an ordinary HTTP server that reads the manifest, fetches the
blobs, checks the bytes hash to what the manifest claims, and serves them. Any
gateway can serve any site, because they all read the same public events.

### Why this works, and why it is not just a fashion

The address is derived from a key, so nobody assigns it and nobody can revoke it.
`https://<npub>.nsite.lol/` is yours because you hold the key, not because an
account exists somewhere.

Nothing is tied to one host. Six public gateways serve the same events today:
nsite.lol, nsite.run, nosto.re, nwb.tf, nsite.cloud, shakespeare.to. If one is
down, change the hostname. If all of them are down, run one yourself; the repo
ships one that fits in a file.

There is no account, no password reset, no billing relationship, and no terms of
service between a person and their own page.

### What nsite-clay adds

An nsite, on its own, is deployed from a terminal like any static site. nsite-clay
makes the page edit and republish *itself*, so the content management system is
inside the static HTML rather than behind it.

You change the DOM. Click around the page and edit text, or open your browser's
inspector and change it there; the page does not care which. The new version is
uploaded to Blossom and one replaceable event is republished saying which hash
`/` now points to. Any gateway renders it.

The idea and the editing model come from [HyperClay](https://hyperclay.com) and
[ClayJS](https://clayjs.com). This is that model with Nostr underneath instead of
a hosting platform.

---

## 2. The philosophy, briefly

**The document is the database.** There is no separate store. A checklist's state
is checkboxes in the markup, a board's cards are elements, a theme is an attribute.
Save the page and open the file in a text editor: everything is right there, in
HTML, readable by a person.

**The file at rest is the state.** No hydration step, no build. `curl` returns the
page as a reader sees it, which means crawlers index it and agents can read it
without executing anything.

**Ownership is a keypair.** "Who may edit this page" is a signature check, not a
row in somebody's users table.

**One key writes the document.** There is no shared editing, no per-visitor
content, and no conflict resolution. Two devices editing at once will lose one
side's work. Say this early rather than building toward it.

### Two places to put things

Relays are also a database, and confusing the two is the main way a page goes
wrong. The rule, in full at [docs/state.md](https://github.com/jooray/nsite-clay/blob/main/docs/state.md):

**The document holds what the page is.** Layout, copy, settings, application
state. A kanban board is the page; it has no life anywhere else.

**Relays hold what you published.** A blog post, a note, a photo: things with an
identity of their own that belong in every Nostr client, not only on this page.
Put a post only in the markup and Habla, njump and the rest never see it.

**A post can be both**, and usually should be. Publish the event, then bake a
rendered copy into the page with `nc.compose.bake(event)`. The markup carries
`nc:from="naddr1…"`, so the page is self-contained and readable with no
JavaScript and no relay, while the post stays a first-class Nostr object.
`nc.compose.refreshBaked()` pulls the copies back in line after an edit elsewhere.

**Neither** holds a draft, a filter or a scroll position. That is what the tab is
doing, not state. Serialisation captures attributes, so anything you put in
`dataset` is published to everyone, forever.

---

## 3. What you are actually building

One `index.html`. It links three files from the site root and nothing else:

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/nsite-clay-base.css">
<script src="/nsite-clay.js"></script>
<script src="/nsite-clay-chrome.js"></script>
```

Your job is the markup, the styling and the words. Sign-in, saving, versions,
media upload, feeds and the post composer already exist. Writing your own is the
commonest mistake; check the runtime reference before implementing anything.

Never copy `nsite-clay.js` or `nsite-clay-base.css` into the site. They live at
the root so one upgrade fixes every page.

And the part that is easiest to leave out: the page has to be one they can *add*
to, not only one they can retype. Every list on it needs a way to put another
item in, every page needs the content form, and a page that grows needs a block
library. That is §8, it is not optional, and it is the difference between a site
somebody owns and a picture of one.

---

## 4. Start from a template

Do not start from a blank file.

```bash
npx nsite-clay init mysite --template=blog --npub=npub1…
npx nsite-clay deploy mysite --sec=nsec1…
```

Pick by what the page is *for*, then redesign it. The template gives you a
working page with the chrome wired up; the design is yours to change.

Ten of the twelve carry a block library, so an owner can add sections you did
not think of. `gallery` and `irc` do not, on purpose. Check yours with
`node tools/template-blocks.mjs <name>`.

| Template | For | Look |
|---|---|---|
| `cms` | a page assembled from blocks rather than a fixed design | warm paper, one column, generous air; the owner adds and reorders blocks in the browser |
| `personal` | one person: who you are, what you write | deep blue-black, gold accent, articles as cards and notes as a timeline |
| `blog` | someone who already writes on Nostr | black, lunar, slow glow; articles in the main column, notes in a sidebar |
| `project` | a piece of software | warm paper and clay-red, numbered bands, terminal cards for the commands |
| `event` | a meetup, a gathering, a date and a place | black and white, poster-scale date and venue, downloadable calendar file |
| `links` | one page holding everything you publish | a contents page with numbered rows and printed destinations, not a stack of buttons |
| `gallery` | photographs | four rooms over one set: a canvas you drag, a sparse hang, a constellation, a plain column |
| `terminal` | a project, for people who like terminals | a shell session, phosphor green, readable top to bottom without pressing anything |
| `phrack` | a long technical write-up | a text file: monospace, 79 columns, ASCII rules, two colours |
| `brutal` | a manifesto, a zine, a loud event | thick borders, hard shadows, oversized type, flat colour |
| `eco` | an essay or a small studio | system fonts, almost no images, measures and prints its own page weight |
| `irc` | a log someone keeps adding to: notes, a journal, a changelog | a channel transcript, monospace, with a composer that appends a line and saves it |

Each is a complete page you can read for the pattern. Their rules are in
[CONTRACT.md](https://github.com/jooray/nsite-clay/blob/main/templates/_shared/CONTRACT.md),
which is short and binding: shared stylesheet from the root, `nc:edit-gate="hash"`,
the standard toolbar markup, CSS variables as the styling hook, no CDN links, no
autosave.

### Choosing when they are not sure

Ask what the page replaces. "My Linktree" is `links`. "My blog" is `blog` if they
post to Nostr already and `personal` if they mostly want an about page. "Our
project's site" is `project`, or `terminal` if the audience lives in one. "A
poster for a thing happening" is `event`. If they want to show pictures, `gallery`.
If they are a writer who cares about typography and hates decoration, `phrack` or
`eco`.

### Always ask

- **Their npub.** Required: it goes in `nc:owner` and it is the only key that can
  ever change the page. Without a Nostr key nothing works.
- **What the page is for.** This picks the template.
- **What should come from Nostr**, if anything: their notes, their articles,
  their photos, somebody else's.
- **What a stranger should do after thirty seconds.** Read something, come to a
  thing, hire them, follow them, zap them.
- **What they do not want.** Most people have a strong opinion about at least one
  thing they hate on websites, and it is cheaper to hear it now.

Also tell them, without being asked, that one key writes the document: there is
no shared editing and no second account.

### Ask as well, for a personal homepage

- Whether the page pulls their notes, their long-form posts, or both. Fetch a
  sample first and design for what is actually there rather than what you
  assumed: someone posting twice a day in two languages needs a different layout
  from someone publishing an essay a month.
- What is at the top: a photo, a sentence, a list of what they are doing now.
- Which links matter, and whether they want a Lightning address on the page.

Take the picture, banner, name, about line, website and Lightning address from
their kind-0 profile rather than asking again. Everything above is judgement they
have and you do not.

---

## 4b. When they already have a page

Sometimes nobody wants a template. They have a page: a hand written one, an
export from a static site generator, a landing page somebody built them years
ago. Do not rebuild it from a template and do not talk them out of the design
they have. Convert it, and leave them something they can add to on their own.

The design is the easy half. The half that decides whether this was worth doing
is §8: a converted page where the owner can fix a typo but cannot add next
month's event is a screenshot of their old site, not a site.

### First, whether it can be converted at all

Say so early rather than halfway through.

- **A page a framework renders at runtime.** React, Vue, Svelte and anything
  else that builds its DOM from JavaScript on load. A save serialises the
  rendered DOM, so what gets published is a snapshot of one render, and on the
  next load the framework re-renders over it and the edits are gone. These are
  not candidates. Their build output usually is, if it is genuinely static HTML.
- **Anything that redraws itself on a timer.** A carousel, a clock, a widget
  that polls. Whatever it happens to be showing at the moment of the save is
  what gets published. Fine for a page where that region is decoration; not fine
  where it is the content.
- **Assets on somebody else's server.** Fonts from a CDN, an analytics script,
  an image hotlinked from elsewhere. They keep working, and they also mean the
  page is only as durable as those hosts, which is the thing an nsite exists to
  avoid. Download them into the directory you are going to deploy, or inline
  them. Google Fonts in particular should be replaced with a system stack. The
  analytics and the cookie banner that existed to declare it can both go.
- **A `<script>` in the page** is saved verbatim and runs for every reader. That
  is the point, and it is also worth reading before you publish somebody else's
  file.

### Second, how many pages

The source is usually a site rather than a page: a home page, an about page, an
index of events, one page per event, an index of posts, one page per post. Three
ways to land that, and this is the decision that costs the most to undo.

**One page.** Sections instead of routes, and the navigation becomes in-page
anchors. Right more often than it looks: a small site's five pages are usually
four paragraphs and two lists, and one document is one thing to edit, one save,
and one place where everything is.

**A page per page.** Each document is its own file with its own `nc:path`, its
own toolbar and its own editing session. Choose it when the pages are genuinely
separate and other people link to them. Then write all of them. A link to a page
you did not build is a link to nothing, and the owner cannot make that page
appear from inside the browser.

**Posts on Nostr rather than in the file.** A blog is the case where the
document is the wrong home for the content. Publish the articles as kind 30023
events and let the page draw them with a feed widget (§10). Adding a post is then
the composer that already exists, the posts appear in Habla and njump as well as
on the page, and nothing has to be deployed to publish one. Bake copies into the
page with `nc.compose.bake()` if it must read with scripting off.

That last route is for writing that has a life of its own. The runtime draws
notes, articles and pictures and nothing else, so a calendar of events, a list of
staff, a price table and a room booking stay markup in the document, and §8 is
how they become things the owner can add to.

### If it is more than one document

- **Every document declares its own `nc:path`**, naming exactly where it lives:
  `/index.html`, `/coworking/index.html`, `/blog/index.html`. A page that
  misreports it compares itself against somebody else's bytes and reloads
  forever, and a page that omits it claims to be `/index.html` and overwrites
  the home page on its first save.
- **Link to a directory with the trailing slash**, `href="/coworking/"`. A
  gateway resolves that to `/coworking/index.html` the way any web server does.
  `/coworking` without the slash is a different path with nothing at it.
- **Deploy the whole directory in one command.** A manifest is the entire path
  table and the CLI builds it from the files on disk, so every page, every
  picture and the three shared files land in one signed event. Deploying one
  file at a time is what produces a site whose pages cannot see each other.
- **A link to a page that does not exist does not stop a save.** The page
  publishes, and the runtime lists the addresses that lead nowhere in a panel
  that stays until it is dismissed, with a button that copies the list. Write
  the pages, or fix the links, and save again. The one thing that still refuses
  is a save that would leave the document unable to load `/nsite-clay.js` or
  `/nsite-clay-chrome.js`, because the page that would repair that is the page
  that no longer loads.

### The conversion itself

**One. Attributes on `<html>`.**

```html
<html lang="en"
      nc:owner="npub1…"
      nc:edit-gate="hash"
      nc:path="/index.html">
```

`nc:owner` is the only required one. `nc:edit-gate="hash"` keeps the controls
away from readers, and `nc:path` has to name where this document actually lives
(see above, and §12). Relays and Blossom servers have working defaults; set
`nc:relays` and `nc:servers` only if they have their own.

**Two. The three shared files, at the site root, deployed with the page.**

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/nsite-clay-base.css">
<script src="/nsite-clay.js"></script>
<script src="/nsite-clay-chrome.js"></script>
```

Not from a CDN, and not pasted into the document. They are files in their site,
uploaded to Blossom and named in their manifest like everything else.

The stylesheet is only needed for the runtime's own dialogs and rails. Their CSS
is untouched by it; it defines variables and styles elements whose names all
start with `nc-`.

**Three. The toolbar**, copied verbatim from
[CONTRACT.md](https://github.com/jooray/nsite-clay/blob/main/templates/_shared/CONTRACT.md)
near the end of `<body>`. Without it there is no way to sign in or save from the
page, and a person who cannot find the save button has not been given a
self-editable site. Keep the `data-nc-cms` button in it: the shared stylesheet
hides that one until the page has an `nc:cms` block, so it costs nothing on a
page that does not yet have one and appears by itself when it does.

**Four. `editable` on everything a person would change.** §8, layer one. On a
converted page this is the bulk of the typing and none of the thinking: walk the
document top to bottom and mark every heading, paragraph, caption, list row,
button label, date, price and address. Twenty is a low count for a home page.
Do not stop after the hero.

**Five. Every list becomes a list they can add to.** §8, layer two, and the step
that separates a conversion from a screenshot. Whatever the source page repeats
is a shape that needs Add, Duplicate, Delete and reorder: the events, the posts,
the people, the links, the opening hours. You have the shapes in front of you,
so there is nothing to invent.

**Six. The content form.** An `nc:cms` rules block covering the whole page, with
a card list for every repeating shape. §8 again. Do this on every conversion
rather than only on the ones that look like a CMS, because the person who
inherits the page did not write it and will not know where to click.

**Seven. Blocks.** A converted page usually already contains its own library:
the sections that repeat are the shapes. Wrap the region that should grow in
`nc:blocks`, give each existing section an `nc:block-type`, and lift one of each
distinct shape into a `<template nc:block>` (§9b). Do not invent shapes and do
not add CSS the page does not already use. A block added next March has to come
out looking like the ones that are there today, and on a converted page you have
the answer in front of you.

**Eight. Deploy the whole directory** (§5), then open the published page with
`#edit` and go down the list at the end of §8. Do that before handing anything
over: the checks are all things the owner will try in their first five minutes.

### One thing worth knowing

The runtime does not only save what was typed into an `editable` region. A save
serialises the live DOM, so a change made from the browser's own inspector, from
the console, or by the page's own script is published like any other. Nothing
notices such a change by default, though, so autosave will not fire and the
unload guard will not warn about it. A page whose own code edits itself can add
`nc:watch-dom` to `<html>` to have those count as edits too. Leave it off
otherwise: on a page with a clock in it, it would mark the page unsaved forever.

---

## 5. Getting it online

Two routes to the same three steps. Pick by who is doing it.

**They publish, in a browser.** <https://nsite-clay.cypherpunk.today/deploy.html>
picks a template, signs in or generates a key with a NIP-49 backup file, checks
what is already at that path, uploads the files and signs the manifest. Nothing
to install. Send a person there when they only want one of the twelve templates
with their own words in it, and point them at
<https://nsite-clay.cypherpunk.today/guide.html> for the walkthrough with
screenshots. You do not need to do anything in that case.

**You publish, from a terminal.** This is the route when you have *built*
something: a design of your own, a block library, a page that is an app. The
publisher only ships the templates that are on the project site; a page you wrote
has to go up from where you wrote it.

```bash
npx nsite-clay deploy mysite --sec=nsec1…                    # a raw key
NOSTR_BUNKER_URI="bunker://…" npx nsite-clay deploy mysite   # a remote signer
```

Prefer the bunker. It keeps the key off the machine running the deploy, which
matters when that machine is yours rather than theirs. Pass the URI in the
environment, never as an argument: an argument is visible to every process on the
box.

The page lands at `https://<their npub>.nsite.lol/`. `--site=blog` makes a
second, separate site under the same key.

`deploy` takes a directory, not a file, and publishes the whole of it as one
signed path table. That is how a site with more than one page has to go up: the
manifest names every document, every picture and the three shared files at once,
and a page whose sibling is not in the table has a link that leads nowhere. Lay
the directory out the way the URLs read, `index.html` at the root and
`coworking/index.html` for `/coworking/`, and give every document its own
`nc:path`.

You will not have their key, and should not ask for one. Two ways round it:
build the directory, hand it over and let them run the one deploy command; or
have them paste a `bunker://` URI from their signer, which signs without the key
ever reaching your machine. Either way, after the first deploy the page publishes
itself and they never need either route again.

A custom domain is a CNAME to the *npub subdomain*, not to the gateway, because
the npub is what the gateway reads out of the hostname:
`blog.example.com CNAME npub1….nsite.lol`. Do not promise HTTPS on it. The public
gateways hold a wildcard for their own domain only, so a browser asking for
`https://blog.example.com` gets a TLS `unrecognized name` alert. Say plain HTTP,
or a gateway they run themselves.

Develop against the local stack rather than public infrastructure:

```bash
npm run devnet     # relay, Blossom and gateway on localhost, all in memory
```

Deploy into it with `--relays=ws://127.0.0.1:4869 --servers=http://127.0.0.1:4870`
and open `http://<npub>.localhost:4871/`. Browsers resolve anything under
`.localhost` to loopback, so the npub sits in the hostname exactly as in
production. Stop the process and everything it held is gone.

After the first deploy the page publishes itself and they never need a terminal
again. Tell them that.

---

## 6. Signing in: recommend a remote signer

Three ways in. Steer them to the second.

1. **A NIP-07 browser extension**, Alby or nos2x. Fine on their own machine.
2. **A remote signer over NIP-46**, Amber on Android or nsec.app. The key stays on
   their phone and every save is approved there. The right default for a page
   served by a gateway, and what you should suggest first.
3. **Pasting a key into the page.** It works, stays in the tab, is written
   nowhere, and is still the weakest option. Say so rather than defaulting to it.

The toolbar handles all three. You write no sign-in code. The sign-in QR is
generated in the page, so the connection secret never leaves the browser.

Do not ask for their nsec. You do not need it and you should not have it.

---

## 7. The edit gate

Every template ships `nc:edit-gate="hash"` on `<html>`. Readers see the page and
nothing to click. The owner adds `#edit` to the URL and the toolbar appears.

Tell them explicitly, because a page with no visible way in looks broken to
someone who has forgotten:

```
https://<their npub>.nsite.lol/#edit
```

Put it in the handover note. `nc.settings.open()` turns the gate off for someone
who would rather have the toolbar always visible.

Autosave is off, deliberately: every save stores the whole page again and files a
version, so a timer publishes a dozen versions of one paragraph. Leaving with
unsaved work already warns them.

---

## 8. Making a page editable

The section people skim, and the one that decides whether what you built is a
website or a picture of one. A page whose owner can fix a typo but cannot add
next month's event comes back to you within a month, or dies quietly.

Three layers. A page is finished when it has all three, and not before.

### Layer one: the words

- `editable` on a container: rich text, where Enter starts a paragraph and
  selecting text raises a toolbar with headings, lists, quotes, links, pictures,
  video and Nostr feeds.
- `editable="single-line"` on a heading, a caption or a list row: no Enter, no
  block menu.

Use `single-line` for anything whose element is inline, an `<a>` that is a
button, a `<span>`, a `<cite>`. Those cannot legally hold a paragraph, and the
runtime relies on the token to keep one out.

Mark everything a person would plausibly want to change, and read "everything"
literally: every heading, every paragraph, every caption, the label on every
button, the address in the footer, the line under the logo, the dates, the
prices, the quotes, the names. Twenty editable regions is a low count for a
content page. The question is not whether they would want to change a given
line, it is whether there is a reason it must never change, and there rarely is.

Form controls persist by default, because that is what "the document is the
database" means: a checked box is still checked for the next visitor. Put
`nc:no-persist` on a search box or a filter, where baking the last value into
the published file would be wrong.

### Layer two: the things there is more than one of

Name every kind of thing on the page. An event, a post, a person, a photograph,
a link, a price, an opening time. For each one, ask whether the owner can add
another one next month with nobody's help. Where the answer is no, you have
built a brochure with editable text, and the first thing they ask for will be
the thing you left out.

Every repeating shape gets four operations: add, duplicate, delete and reorder.
Two mechanisms provide them, they cost a few lines each, and a page should have
both, because they suit different people and different moments.

**A gear on the item**, for the person looking at the page who wants to change
the thing in front of them:

```html
<section class="events">
  <h2 editable="single-line">What is coming up</h2>

  <div class="event-list">
    <article class="event">
      <p class="event-when" editable="single-line">27 May, 19:00</p>
      <h3 class="event-title" editable="single-line">Agentic organisations</h3>
      <div class="event-body" editable><p>An evening about what happens when…</p></div>
      <menu class="nc-gear nc-gear-row">
        <button type="button" onclick="nc.dom.cloneClosest(this, '.event')">Duplicate</button>
        <button type="button" onclick="nc.dom.moveClosest(this, -1, '.event')">Up</button>
        <button type="button" onclick="nc.dom.moveClosest(this, 1, '.event')">Down</button>
        <button type="button" onclick="nc.dom.removeClosestAsk(this, '.event', 'this event')">Delete</button>
      </menu>
    </article>
  </div>

  <menu class="nc-gear nc-gear-row">
    <button type="button" onclick="nc.dom.addFrom('tpl-event', '.event-list')">Add an event</button>
  </menu>
</section>

<template id="tpl-event">
  <article class="event">
    <p class="event-when" editable="single-line">A date</p>
    <h3 class="event-title" editable="single-line">The name of it</h3>
    <div class="event-body" editable><p>What it is.</p></div>
    <menu class="nc-gear nc-gear-row">…the same four buttons…</menu>
  </article>
</template>
```

Two details in there are the ones that go wrong. `.event-list` holds events and
nothing else, because `addFrom` appends: a container that also held the heading
and the Add button would take the new event after the button. And the shape
lives in a `<template>`, which renders nothing, is saved with the page, and
gives the owner an empty event rather than a copy of last month's.

Repeat this for every shape on the page. A page with events, posts and people
has three of these, not one.

**A card list in the content form**, for the person who would rather fill in
fields than click into a page, which is most people who did not write it. That
is the next part.

### Layer three: the sections nobody thought of

A block library, §9b. The owner adds whole sections in your design, months after
you have gone. Ten of the twelve shipped templates carry one, and a converted
page nearly always should.

### The content form, and why every page should have one

Editing in place suits whoever wrote the page. It does not suit the person who
inherits it and wants to change the price, the date and the third paragraph
without hunting for them, and it gives them nowhere at all to press "add". So
describe the page's fields in a rules block and let the runtime generate a form:

```html
<script type="application/json" nc:cms>
{
  "title":  ".site-title",
  "hero":   "img.hero@src",
  "open":   ".status@data-open",
  "tags":   ".tag[]",
  "events": [".event", {
    "date":  ".event-when",
    "title": ".event-title",
    "text":  ".event-body",
    "link":  "a.event-link@href"
  }],
  "people": [".person", { "name": ".person-name", "role": ".person-role" }]
}
</script>
```

The button is already in the toolbar in
[CONTRACT.md](https://github.com/jooray/nsite-clay/blob/main/templates/_shared/CONTRACT.md):

```html
<button class="nc-owner-only" data-nc-cms>Edit content</button>
```

Leave it in whether or not the page has rules yet. The shared stylesheet hides
it until there is an `nc:cms` block, so it appears by itself the day one is
added.

`nc.cms.open()` draws a panel down the right hand side with one control per
field. Typing writes straight through to the element and marks the page unsaved;
the panel itself is `nc:chrome`, so it is never part of the file. The rules are,
because they are part of the page.

The grammar:

| Written as | Means |
|---|---|
| `".title"` | the element's text |
| `"img.hero@src"`, `".x@data-y"` | an attribute, with a picture picker when it is an `<img src>` |
| `".agree@checked"` | a checkbox, which persists like any other input |
| `".tag[]"` | one field per matching element, with Add and Remove |
| `[".post", { … }]` | a card per match, with Add, Duplicate, Remove and reorder |
| `{ "author": { … } }` | a labelled group, purely for tidiness |

The card list is the one that matters and the one to reach for by default. Every
repeating shape on the page should appear as one, so the panel offers "Add
events" beside the events and "Add people" beside the people. Add copies the
last item, so a new event arrives in the page's own design with last month's
words in it, ready to type over.

For a list that can legitimately be emptied, keep one item as the shape to copy
and mark it `nc:cms-template hidden`. It is never offered as content, and Add
clones it rather than the last item. Give it an ordinary class as well, say
`class="event event-shape"`, and point the gears at `.event:not(.event-shape)`,
so reordering does not count a hidden element nobody can see.

Write rules for the whole page rather than for the parts you found interesting.
A field that is not in the rules is a field the owner has to go and find.

### Before you hand it over

Open the published page with `#edit`, sign in as the owner, and answer these
without opening a text editor:

- Can I change every word I can see?
- Can I add a second one of every kind of thing on this page? The events, the
  posts, the people, the links?
- Can I delete one, and put them in a different order?
- Can I add a section that is not on the page yet?
- Can I change a picture, and put a new one in?
- Does "Edit content" list everything on the page, and does Add work in every
  list it shows?
- Does Save go through, and does the page still look right after a reload?

Every "no" is work that is not finished. These are the first five minutes of
somebody's ownership of their own site.

---

## 9. When the page is an app, not a document

A board, a checklist or a directory needs more than typing. Put the controls on
the thing they act on and mark them `nc-gear`, so they appear only for a
signed-in owner who is editing:

```html
<article class="card" data-status="active">
  <h3 editable="single-line">Fix Blossom sync</h3>
  <menu class="nc-gear nc-gear-row">
    <button type="button" onclick="nc.dom.cloneClosest(this, '.card')">Duplicate</button>
    <button type="button" onclick="nc.dom.moveClosest(this, -1, '.card')">Up</button>
    <button type="button" onclick="nc.dom.removeClosestAsk(this, '.card', 'this card')">Delete</button>
  </menu>
</article>
```

**Do not put `clay="no-save"` on a gear.** That strips it from the save, so the
pattern works exactly once and the published page has no controls. A gear is part
of the app and belongs in the file; the rules above keep it away from readers.
`clay="no-save"` is for markup that must never be written at all, such as a
composer holding a half-typed line. To have a control that both persists and is
never itself written, draw it from a script that persists.

`nc.dom` gives you `clone`, `remove`, `move`, `moveTo`, `insert`, `addFrom` a
`<template>`, `toggle` and `set`, plus `cloneClosest` and friends so a control
addresses the block it sits in. Every one arms the new markup for editing and
marks the page unsaved, which is the bookkeeping you would otherwise forget.

`move` reorders within one parent. A card going from one column to the next
crosses parents, so that is `moveTo(el, container)` or, from a gear,
`moveToClosest(this, '.card', '.col-cards', 1)`, which steps through the
containers in document order. The node itself travels, so anything typed into it
comes along.

Point those at a container that holds **only** the items. `moveTo` appends, so a
column whose element also contains a heading and an "Add" button would take the
card after the button. Give the column an inner `.col-cards` and target that.

```html
<menu class="nc-gear nc-gear-row">
  <button type="button" onclick="nc.dom.moveToClosest(this, '.card', '.col', -1)">&larr;</button>
  <button type="button" onclick="nc.dom.moveToClosest(this, '.card', '.col', 1)">&rarr;</button>
</menu>
```

Read the document back as data with `nc.dom.all(".card")` and
`nc.dom.by(".card", "data-status")`. The DOM is the query engine; there is no
model to keep in sync with the view, because the view is the model.

State with no visual form goes in a JSON block through `nc.state.get()`,
`.set()` and `.update()`, which escapes the closing tag that would otherwise end
the block and the rest of your page.

`nc.dom` calls `nc.editable.refresh()` for you. You need it yourself only for
markup you inserted some other way, before focusing it, or the new region will
not be typeable.

### The controls, and where the rest of this lives

A gear belongs to one card or one row. A block (§9b) is a whole section. The
content form (§8) is the same page seen as fields, and it is where a repeating
shape gets its Add button for whoever would rather not click into the page. Most
pages want all three, and they mix freely; `templates/cms/index.html` uses them
together.

### What an app here can and cannot do

This layer exists because of HyperClay, which makes a single HTML file editable
by its owner and lets that file be a real application. It is worth knowing
exactly where the two part company, because the wrong assumption in either
direction wastes an afternoon.

**Your own JavaScript survives the save.** A save is a serialisation of the live
DOM with a short list of removals, not a pass through a sanitiser. Inline
`onclick` handlers, `<script>` blocks, `<template>` elements, custom attributes
and data attributes are all authored markup and come back byte for byte. The
sanitiser guards two doors only: HTML pasted into an editable region, and
content fetched from a relay. Neither one touches what you wrote.

**What the save does remove**, and therefore what you can rely on being absent
from the published file: anything marked `clay="no-save"`, anything the runtime
injected (`nc:chrome`), anything fetched at view time (`nc:transient`), and the
runtime's own state attributes on `<html>`. Everything else stays.

**A gear must not carry the page's own layout class.** `.nc-gear` hides with
`!important` and the reveal rule restores it the same way, because a page
stylesheet loads after the shared one and a gear that lost that fight would show
its controls to every reader. So `class="nc-gear chips"` will not get your
`display: flex`. Use `nc-gear-row` for a row of buttons, or write your own rule
against `html[nc\:owner-here="true"][nc\:editing="true"]`.

**Anything a script does for the current view alone must be undone before the
save**, because the save serialises the DOM as it stands. `nc:no-persist` covers
an input's value and nothing else: a class your filter hangs on hidden cards, or
a `data-theme` you applied from `nc.state`, will be written into the file as
though someone had authored it. Strip those in `nc.addDocumentTransform(clone =>
…)`, which runs on the copy being saved and cannot affect what the reader is
looking at.

**Form state is persisted for you.** HyperClay asks for a `persist` attribute on
an input. Here it is the default: a checkbox the owner ticks, a value typed into
a text field and a selected option are all written into the outgoing file. Opt a
control out with `nc:no-persist`, which is what a search box wants so a
half-typed filter is not published. Password and file inputs are never written.

**One writer, and the writer is a key.** HyperClay logs an owner in against a
server; here the page checks a signature, so there is no account and no server
to run. The consequence is that only the key holder can save. A visitor can
change the page in front of them, and nothing they do reaches anyone else.
Anything that needs a stranger's input to be recorded belongs on relays, as a
Nostr event they sign themselves, not in the document.

**No conflict detection.** Two devices editing under one key will lose one
side's work. Version history means it can be recovered, not that it cannot
happen.

**Every save republishes the whole document.** This is the real budget. A page
that saves on every keystroke, or one that grows without bound because a script
appends to it, becomes expensive to load and slow to publish. Keep the document
the size of a document.

**No server-side anything.** No request handling, no scheduled work, no secrets.
A key in the file is a key you have published.

---

## 9b. Blocks: a page they can extend without you

A finished page is a page that goes stale, because the next thing they want to
add is a thing you did not build. Blocks are the answer: you design the page, and
they add sections to it afterwards, in your design, with no editor and no you.

Mark the container. Every element child of it is a block:

```html
<main nc:blocks>
  <section nc:block-type="intro">…</section>
  <section nc:block-type="work">…</section>
</main>
```

In edit mode the runtime draws a rail on each block (move, duplicate, configure,
delete) and a `+` between them that opens a palette. The palette is built from
the document's own library, which is a set of inert `<template>` elements:

```html
<template nc:block="picture" nc:label="Picture" nc:icon="▥"
          nc:group="Media" nc:on-add="image" nc:hint="Upload one or paste a URL.">
  <section class="b-picture">
    <figure>
      <img nc:slot src="…" alt="">
      <figcaption editable="single-line">Caption</figcaption>
    </figure>
  </section>
</template>
```

**Write every shape in the page's own markup and classes.** That is the whole
trick and the only part you can get wrong: a block added next March has to come
out looking like the ones you wrote today, so a library for a monospace zine
produces monospace, and one for a card grid produces a card. Do not reach for
generic markup, and do not add CSS for the library that the page does not
already use.

`nc:on-add` runs a picker once the block lands and `nc:slot` marks what it acts
on: `image`, `video`, `feed`, `post`. Backing out of the picker removes the block
again, so a cancelled "add a picture" leaves nothing behind.

A `<template>` renders nothing and is saved with the page, so the library travels
with the file. Whoever opens the document next has the palette, with nothing to
fetch and nothing to install. Nothing the rail draws is written to disk; a reader
gets plain markup.

Ten of the twelve shipped templates carry a library. Read one before writing
yours: `templates/cms/index.html` is the fullest, twelve shapes over four groups,
and it is browsable at <https://nsite-clay.cypherpunk.today/t/cms/>.
`templates/phrack/index.html` and `templates/terminal/index.html` show the same
idea bent hard into a particular design. `gallery` and `irc` deliberately have
none, which is the other lesson: a page whose content is redrawn from a live feed
on every load has nothing persisted to make a block of.

Reach for a block when the owner will want sections you have not thought of.
Reach for a gear (§9) when the control belongs to one card or one row. The two
mix freely; `templates/cms/index.html` uses both.

Check your work: `node tools/template-blocks.mjs <name>` loads the page in a
browser and tests the reader's view, the rails, the insert points, the library,
that adding a block adds one, that nothing the runtime draws reaches a save, and
that the page does not scroll sideways.

---

## 10. Nostr content on the page

A feed is markup. It fetches at view time, verifies every signature in the
browser and sanitises what it shows:

```html
<div nc:feed="articles" nc:authors="npub1…, npub1…" nc:limit="5"
     nc:style="grid" nc:pinned="my-first-post"></div>
```

`nc:feed` is `notes` (kind 1), `articles` (kind 30023) or `images` (kind 20).
Also `nc:limit`, `nc:style` (`list` or `grid`), `nc:min-length` to drop
one-liners, `nc:topic` for a single tag, and `nc:feed-relays` to override.

Pinning an article uses its slug, not its event id: kind 30023 is replaceable, so
the id changes every time the author fixes a typo and an id-pin breaks.

Style feeds by overriding what they emit rather than rebuilding it. Each item is
an `<article class="nc-item">` containing a `<header class="nc-by">` with
`.nc-avatar`, `.nc-name` and `.nc-when` inside it, then the body as a sibling:
`.nc-title` and `.nc-summary` for an article, `.nc-text` for a note, `.nc-pics`
for pictures, and an optional `<footer class="nc-tags">`. Add `nc-feed-cards` to
the widget for boxed items and `nc-feed-spread` to push the date to the right;
without them an item is a plain line, which is what a log or a list wants.

A display name comes from a kind-0 profile and is free text: some are a whole
sentence. The base stylesheet clips `.nc-name`, so do not undo that unless you
have somewhere for a long one to go.

A feed is fetched, not stored, so a save keeps the widget's configuration and
none of the posts. A reader with scripting off sees an empty block. Design for
that, or bake the posts in as well.

The composer (`nc.compose.open()`) lists what the owner has published and writes
more: short notes and long-form articles, with an option to bake a copy into the
page as it publishes.

---

### Where a post opens

`nc:open-with` on a feed decides what a click does. Leave it out and the post
opens in the page, which is usually what you want: the event is already there
from drawing the card, so it costs no relay call, and closing it does not
navigate. Otherwise `yakihonne`, `primal`, `njump`, or a URL of your own with
`{id}`, `{npub}`, `{kind}` and `{d}` in it.

Do not assemble those URLs yourself. An article and a note are at different
paths in every one of these clients, and the name picks the right one:

    yakihonne  /article/<naddr>   /note/<nevent>
    primal     /a/<naddr>         /e/<nevent>
    njump      /<naddr>           /<nevent>

## 11. The design is yours to write

There is no theme system, no skin, no config. A page is one HTML file and you
write its CSS, so whatever you can build in HTML and CSS is what the page looks
like: a poster, a zine in 79 monospace columns, a shell session, a photo wall.
All twelve shipped templates are that and nothing more, which is why they look
nothing like each other.

The runtime draws a few surfaces of its own, and they follow you rather than the
other way round. Set the variables and the toolbar, the dialogs, the version
list, the pickers, the text toolbar, the toasts, the feeds, the block rails and
the post reader all come out in your palette. You never restyle the chrome
directly and you never fight it.

So the job for a page somebody asked you for is: pick the nearest template as a
starting point, or start from `cms` if the shape is "a page", write the design,
write the words, mark what is editable, and give it a block library so they can
add to it later. Then §5 to get it online.

Work in this order; it saves rewriting.

1. **The variables.** `--nc-ink`, `--nc-ink-dim`, `--nc-bg`, `--nc-panel`,
   `--nc-edge`, `--nc-accent`, `--nc-accent-ink`, `--nc-ok`, `--nc-bad`,
   `--nc-radius`, `--nc-radius-sm`, `--nc-shadow`, `--nc-chrome-font`,
   `--nc-mono`. `--nc-ok` and `--nc-bad` drive the toolbar's status dot, so a
   template that leaves them gets a green and red that may clash with its
   palette. These reach every surface the
   runtime draws: the toolbar, the dialogs, the version list, the pickers, the
   floating text toolbar, the toasts and the feeds. A square, shadowless design
   sets `--nc-radius: 0` and `--nc-shadow: none` and the chrome squares off with
   it.
2. **The content.** Real words. Mark everything editable.
3. **The layout and type.** Your own rules, under the variables.
4. **The feeds.** Restyle, do not rebuild.
5. **The gears and the content form.** Every repeating shape gets both, §8.
6. **The block library.** Last, because it copies the shapes you just settled.

Images: a page that phones home is not a page they own, so no CDN, no third
party fonts, no analytics. An SVG inline or as a `data:` URI costs one request
of zero bytes and cannot go away. A photograph goes on Blossom, where the rest
of the page already lives, either through the picture picker or by deploying it
alongside the document.

---

## 12. Things that will bite you

- **A link to a page that is not in the site does not stop a save.** The page
  publishes, and the runtime shows the addresses that lead nowhere in a panel
  that stays until it is dismissed, with a button that copies the list. It is a
  list of work, not a failure. What still refuses is a save that would leave the
  document unable to load `/nsite-clay.js` or `/nsite-clay-chrome.js`, because
  the page that would repair that is the page that no longer loads. Deploy the
  whole directory with the CLI rather than hand-editing the path table.
- **A directory link needs its trailing slash.** A gateway reads `/coworking/`
  as `/coworking/index.html`, the way any web server does. `/coworking` is a
  different path, and there is nothing at it.
- **Every page needs its own `nc:path`.** A document defaults to `/index.html`,
  so a site with more than one editable page, an about page, a translation,
  anything, needs `nc:path="/about.html"` on each `<html>` or saving one of them
  overwrites another. This is silent until someone loses a page.
- **Assets are content-fingerprinted.** `/logo-9f2a1e.png` changes when the file
  changes. Never hardcode a fingerprint you saw once.
- **Relays disagree.** Publish to several, and include `wss://relay.nsite.lol` so
  the gateway sees changes promptly. Verify retention by reading your own events
  back: some relays accept a publish and store nothing.
- **Blossom servers are picky.** Several refuse `text/html`. `cdn.hzrd149.com` and
  `blossom.primal.net` work.
- **`relay.damus.io` has been unreliable.** Do not put it first.
- **One key, no conflict detection.** Two devices editing at once lose one side's
  work.
- **The gateway is trusted for the first byte.** Everything the document loads
  afterwards is hash-checked and every event is signature-checked, but the entry
  document cannot verify itself. Running a local gateway removes the trust.

---

## 13. Writing

The words matter more than the design and they are the part most often left as
filler. No em or en dashes. No "there are several ways to". No sentence that
announces what the next sentence is about to do. No "crucial", "seamless",
"robust", "vibrant". Write what the page is, for someone who has not seen it.

If the page is in a language other than English, write it as a native speaker
would, with that language's punctuation and typography. Slovak and Czech take
`„…"` quotation marks and a spaced en dash rather than an em dash, sentence-case
headings, lowercase months, a decimal comma and a space before `%`.

Those rules are the short list. The long one is
[humanizer](https://github.com/jooray/humanizer), a skill that names the habits
which mark prose as machine-written and says what to write instead: inflated
symbolism, promotional adjectives, vague attribution, the rule of three, the
sentence that says a thing is not merely X but Y. It has its own section for
Slovak and Czech, where the giveaway is usually an English draft translated word
by word. If you have it, run the page's words through it before you hand the
page over.

---

## 14. Handing it over

Tell them, in this order:

1. The address of their page.
2. The same address with `#edit`, which is how they get the controls.
3. How to add a thing, by name: "Edit content in the toolbar has an Add button
   under Events", or "the Add an event button at the end of the list". Say it
   about each kind of thing on the page. This is the question they will actually
   have, and a page that can do it but never said so is a page that cannot.
4. Which key controls it, and that losing it means losing the ability to change
   the page.
5. That the page now updates itself and they will not need a terminal again.

That is the whole operating manual.
